title: Building My Own Small Inference Cloud
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: A Local Workbench for Running LLM Inference Experiments on OCI
https://github.com/aruanurag/llm-inference-lab/tree/main/apps/oci-inference-cloud

Over the last few articles, I have been learning and writing about LLM inference systems. I started with concepts like KV cache, batching, GPU utilization, multi-GPU inference, request routing, prefill vs decode, continuous batching, PagedAttention, vLLM architecture, CPU inference, and model routing.
Most of those articles were conceptual. But while writing them and doing hands-on experiments, I noticed something very practical: I was repeating the same setup steps again and again.
Each experiment usually involved:

creating infrastructure
setting up a machine
installing the inference runtime
deploying llama.cpp
downloading a model
starting the server
exposing an endpoint
running benchmarks
comparing results
cleaning up infrastructure
That repetition made me think:

Can I build a small tool
that helps me set up inference experiments faster?
That is where this project started.

The app is an early MVP of a local inference cloud workbench. The goal is simple: provision infrastructure, deploy an inference runtime, expose a local endpoint, run benchmarks, try small apps, compare results, and repeat quickly.
It is not a finished product. It is more like a learning tool that I can keep improving as I move deeper into inference systems.
Why did I build this?
When learning infrastructure-heavy topics, reading alone is not enough. At some point, I want to actually run things.
I want to:

measure latency
compare throughput
test CPU inference
try different model sizes
compare shapes and OCPU counts
eventually move to GPUs
later explore Kubernetes and cluster deployments
But every experiment has setup cost. If setup takes too long, I run fewer experiments. If I run fewer experiments, I learn slower.
So the goal of this tool is to reduce friction. I wanted something that lets me quickly:

create an experiment
pick infrastructure
deploy a model
run inference
benchmark results
try an app
clean everything up
The faster this loop becomes, the more experiments I can run.
What is this app?
The app is called:
OCI Inference Cloud
It is a local hackathon-style workbench for inference experiments. Right now, it focuses on OCI and uses your existing OCI CLI profiles.
The current MVP can:

provision an OCI CPU/HPC instance for an experiment
deploy llama.cpp
expose a private OpenAI-compatible endpoint through a local backend proxy
run benchmark presets
provide sample applications for direct chat and routing experiments
terminate app-created infrastructure from the selected experiment
Instead of manually setting up everything each time, the app gives me a repeatable workflow for running inference experiments.
Why local-first?
This part was important to me. The app is intentionally local-first.
It:

uses existing OCI CLI profiles
does not store OCI API keys
generates SSH keys under ~/.llm-inference-cloud/
keeps benchmark results outside the Git repo
uses SSH tunnels instead of exposing llama-server publicly
can terminate the infrastructure it created for an experiment
That design keeps the system easier to understand, easier to debug, and easier to clean up.
What does it do today?
The current flow looks like this:

Create or select an experiment.
Load OCI context.
Select existing networking.
Provision a CPU/HPC instance.
Deploy llama.cpp.
Select a GGUF model.
Run benchmark presets.
Start the local endpoint proxy.
Try sample apps.
Delete infrastructure when done.
That is already enough to make hands-on inference experimentation much more enjoyable.
The current model catalog includes:

Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct Q4_K_M
Qwen2.5 7B Instruct Q4_K_M
Qwen2.5 7B Instruct Q8_0
Qwen2.5 14B Instruct Q4_K_M
custom directly downloadable GGUF URL
The custom GGUF option is useful because I do not want the tool to be limited to only a few hardcoded models.
Why llama.cpp first?
For the first version, I started with llama.cpp because I wanted to explore CPU inference seriously.
A lot of inference discussions quickly move to GPUs, and GPUs are obviously important. But CPU inference is also interesting for:

smaller models
quantized models
local inference
edge inference
cost-sensitive workloads
experimentation without large GPU infrastructure
It is also just fun. Running your own model, exposing your own endpoint, and talking to it through a small app feels very different from only calling a hosted API.
Why OCI?
Right now, this MVP is based on OCI because that is where I was testing infrastructure and CPU/HPC shapes.
I was also surprised by the performance I was seeing for CPU-based inference. That made the experiment more interesting.
The broader question I wanted to explore was:

How far can we push useful inference
without immediately jumping to GPUs?
This does not mean CPU replaces GPU. That is not the point.
The better mental model is:

Use the right hardware
for the right inference workload.
A small quantized model may work well on CPU. A larger model, long-context workload, or high-throughput serving system may need GPUs. A future inference platform may use both.
The bigger vision
The longer-term idea in my mind is something like a small personal inference cloud.

I was thinking about platforms like Nebius and other AI cloud systems where you can provision inference infrastructure and then connect applications to model endpoints. I wanted a much smaller, learning-focused version of that idea.
A future version could look like this:

Choose cloud.
Choose hardware.
Choose model.
Choose inference engine.
Deploy endpoint.
Run benchmark.
Connect app.
Compare cost and performance.
Today, the app starts with OCI and llama.cpp. Later, I can imagine adding:

GPU inference
vLLM
Kubernetes
multi-node deployments
model routing
benchmark dashboards
observability
cost comparison
experiment history
The current version is only the first step, but it gives me a foundation to keep building on.
What are the sample apps?
Right now, the project includes two simple sample apps.
The first one is a direct CPU chat app. It talks directly to the local endpoint exposed by the OCI inference workbench.
The second one is a router chat app. It can use the CPU endpoint and also connect to an OpenAI model.
This makes it useful for exploring basic routing ideas:

Simple request → local CPU model

More complex request → larger hosted model

This connects nicely to the model routing ideas I have been exploring. Eventually, I want this to become a playground for testing routing strategies, comparing outputs, and understanding when smaller local models are good enough.
What does the architecture look like?
At a high level, the app has two main parts:

Backend
Frontend
The structure looks like this:

apps/oci-inference-cloud/
├── backend/
│   ├── app/
│   ├── tests/
│   └── requirements.txt
└── frontend/
    ├── src/
    └── package.json
The backend and frontend run locally. The OCI instance runs the remote llama-server, but the remote server stays bound to:
on the OCI instance. The local backend reaches it through an SSH tunnel.
The local app exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint like this:
POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/{experiment_id}/endpoint/v1/chat/completions
The simple mental model is:

Browser
  ↓
Local frontend
  ↓
Local backend
  ↓
SSH tunnel
  ↓
Remote llama-server on OCI
So the model server is not publicly exposed. The app talks to it through a local proxy.
Before trying it
You should have:

OCI CLI configured
an OCI profile available
access to create compute instances
existing OCI networking
Python 3
Node.js and npm
Git
The app uses your existing OCI CLI context, so you do not need to paste OCI API keys into the app.
Run the backend
From the repository:

cd apps/oci-inference-cloud/backend
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8090
The backend runs on:
Run the frontend
In another terminal:

cd apps/oci-inference-cloud/frontend
npm install
npm run dev
Open:
Now the local UI should be available.
Create your first experiment
Inside the UI, create or select an experiment.
I like this structure because each test becomes easier to track. For example:

Experiment 1 → Qwen2.5 1.5B on a smaller CPU shape
Experiment 2 → Qwen2.5 7B on a larger CPU shape
Experiment 3 → same model with native build enabled
Experiment 4 → different OCPU count
This makes comparison easier than running disconnected scripts.
Experiment flow
A typical experiment looks like this:

Create or select an experiment.
Load OCI context.
Select existing networking.
Provision a CPU/HPC instance.
Deploy llama.cpp.
Pick a model from the catalog or provide a custom GGUF URL.
Run benchmark presets.
Start the local endpoint proxy.
Use the endpoint from a sample app.
Delete infrastructure when done.
For the first run, I would start with a smaller quantized model. A smaller model gives a faster feedback loop. Once that works, move to larger models and compare behavior.
Native build mode
The app also supports advanced deploy settings.
By default, the portable llama.cpp build is safer because it works across different shapes. But if you want better performance for a specific machine, you can enable native build mode:
-DGGML_NATIVE=ON
This lets llama.cpp compile for the selected shape’s available CPU features.
If native mode fails with:
unsupported instruction 'vpdpbusd'
keep native mode enabled but also enable:
Disable VNNI instructions
in Advanced settings.
This is exactly the kind of hands-on detail that makes experimentation useful. You do not just learn the theory. You learn what actually breaks.
Run benchmarks
After deployment, run benchmark presets.
The app includes a Throughput comparison preset. The recommended flow is:

Create experiment 1.
Deploy llama.cpp.
Run the Throughput comparison preset as the Primary run.
Create experiment 2.
Change one variable.
Run the same preset as the Comparison run.
Review the comparison table.
The important part is:
Change one variable.
For example:

Experiment 1:
Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
Portable build
Shape A

Experiment 2:
Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
Native build
Same shape
Now the comparison is meaningful.
The benchmark comparison focuses on:

approximate output tokens/sec
output characters/sec
requests/sec
p95 latency
p95 TTFT
relative throughput versus the best Primary run
These metrics connect directly to the inference concepts I have been learning: TTFT, latency, throughput, and tokens/sec.
Start the endpoint proxy
After the model is deployed, open the Hackathon view and start the local endpoint proxy.
The generated endpoint looks like this:
CPU_ENDPOINT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/1/endpoint/v1
This is the endpoint the sample apps can use.
Run the direct CPU chat app
The first sample app talks directly to the CPU endpoint:

cd examples/direct-cpu-chat
npm install
CPU_ENDPOINT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/1/endpoint/v1 PORT=3001 npm run dev
Now you can talk to your own model running on the OCI instance.
This is the fun part. After spending so much time reading about inference systems, there is something satisfying about sending a message to your own endpoint and seeing the response come back.
Run the router chat app
The second sample app can use the CPU endpoint and an OpenAI model:

cd examples/router-chat
npm install
CPU_ENDPOINT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/1/endpoint/v1 \
OPENAI_API_KEY=replace-with-your-key \
OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini \
PORT=3002 \
npm run dev
This starts connecting to a bigger idea:
Not every request needs the same model.
A local CPU model may be enough for some requests. A larger hosted model may be better for others.
Eventually, this can evolve into a routing playground:

Simple chat → CPU model
Complex reasoning → hosted model
Private local task → local model
Long analysis → stronger endpoint
That is the type of experiment I want to run more often.
Where is app data stored?
The app stores generated state outside the repo:

~/.llm-inference-cloud/
├── state.db
├── keys/
├── prompts/
├── benchmarks/
└── logs/
This keeps generated keys, logs, prompts, and benchmark results separate from the Git repo.
Cleanup
When the experiment is done, use:
Delete infra
from the selected experiment.
This terminates the app-created OCI infrastructure.
For any tool that provisions cloud resources, cleanup should be part of the normal workflow:

Create experiment
Run benchmark
Save results
Delete infra
Not:

Create experiment
Forget instance
Find surprise bill later
Why this matters for my learning series
This project feels like a transition point in my learning.
The earlier articles helped build the mental model. Now I want to move more toward implementation.
I still want to write conceptual articles, but I also want more hands-on work:

run models
measure latency
compare throughput
test CPU shapes
move to GPUs
deploy with Kubernetes
try routing
visualize benchmark results
This app gives me a small lab environment for future articles.
What comes later?
This MVP starts with OCI, CPU inference, llama.cpp, benchmarks, and two sample apps.
Future improvements could include:

GPU support
vLLM deployments
Kubernetes support
multi-node experiments
better benchmark dashboards
cost comparison
more model catalogs
model routing policies
observability
experiment export
team or hackathon workflows
As I continue the learning series, I want the tool to grow with the topics I am learning.

When I study GPU inference, the app should support GPU experiments. When I study Kubernetes, the app should support Kubernetes deployments. When I study routing, the router app should become more capable. When I study observability, benchmark visualization should improve.
Main idea
The main idea is simple:
Make inference experiments easier to repeat.
Once experiments become easier to repeat, learning becomes faster.
I can test more models, compare more shapes, see real numbers, understand latency and throughput through actual runs, and connect theory with practice.
Final thoughts
This is still an MVP. There will be rough edges, missing features, and many things to improve.
But I am happy with this first version because it solves a real problem in my own learning workflow.
It helps me move from:
reading about inference systems
to:
running inference systems
If you are also learning LLM inference, CPU inference, model serving, or LLMOps, feel free to try it out.
Fork the repo. Run an experiment. Try the sample apps. Open an issue if something breaks. Raise a PR if you want to improve it.
I will keep working on this as I move deeper into GPUs, Kubernetes, routing, and distributed inference.
This is just the first iteration, but it already makes the learning process much more fun.
